---
title: "Design Lab: A Digital Wallet and Double-Entry Ledger"
---

# Design Lab: A Digital Wallet and Double-Entry Ledger

Build a Go wallet simulator with synthetic funds in one currency. The invariant is conservation: every posted transfer has balanced debit and credit entries, and available funds never become negative under the lab's no-overdraft rule.

## Model the ledger first

Store accounts, transfers, and immutable entries. A transfer has a tenant-scoped request ID, source, destination, currency, integer minor-unit amount, and payload hash. Each completed transfer contains equal and opposite signed entries. Keep a cached balance only if it is updated transactionally with those entries and can be verified from them.

Define zero-sum boundaries explicitly. A funding event credits a wallet and debits a designated external-clearing account; money must not appear from an unpaired balance edit. Corrections use reversing entries and a new transfer ID. Never edit posted history to hide an error.

## Go and SQL transaction

Implement `Transfer(ctx, request) (receipt, error)` using one `sql.Tx`:

1. Validate positive amount, supported currency, distinct accounts, and caller authority.
2. Lock both accounts in stable ID order to avoid opposing-transfer lock order.
3. Look up the idempotency request under a uniqueness constraint and verify its payload. Return the prior receipt if already committed.
4. Check available balance and integer overflow limits. Apply debit and credit, append both entries, and store the receipt in the same transaction.
5. Commit and return. On an ambiguous commit response, resolve by the request ID on retry.

Database constraints should enforce positive amounts, account currency compatibility, and uniqueness independently of handlers. Cross-row zero-sum validation needs transactional posting logic or an appropriate database mechanism; a simple column `CHECK` cannot validate an arbitrary multi-row sum.

Go's [transaction guide](https://go.dev/doc/database/execute-transactions) describes the `sql.Tx` lifecycle. Keep every query for this operation on the transaction rather than accidentally calling `db.Exec` mid-transfer.

## Reservations and distribution

Add holds as separate available-versus-posted state. Capture or release a hold once, with an explicit expiry race policy. Do not infer a hold from an unfinished HTTP connection.

The first version requires both accounts on one database so the operation can be atomic. Sharding accounts across databases invalidates that assumption. A later design needs an explicit multi-step settlement protocol, intermediate accounts, recovery states, and reconciliation; sending two unrelated balance updates is insufficient.

## Acceptance evidence

Start account A with 100 synthetic units and B with zero. Run 100 concurrent requests transferring 3 units each, with unique request IDs. Exactly 33 can succeed if no other operations run; A ends at 1 and B at 99. Replay every request, and verify balances do not change.

Crash between inserting the debit and credit before commit, then confirm rollback leaves neither visible. Compare cached balances with ledger sums, and assert every transfer balances to zero. Test reverse-direction concurrent transfers, duplicate IDs with changed amounts, overflow, cancellation, and reconciliation after a lost commit response.
